page.title: Lesson Overview
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 7 | Page 1 of 6

Lesson Overview: Integrated Author Portfolio Preparation

Lesson Focus

Lesson 7: Integrated Author Portfolio Preparation

Primary Standards: MLA.CW.PUB.01 — Online collaborative publication; MLA.CW.COM.01 — Author presentation of creative work.

Supporting Standards: MLA.CW.REV.01 — Revision from feedback; MLA.CW.PUB.02 — Format-specific quality work; MLA.CW.WR.08 — Reflection on creative process and product.

What You Will Learn

  • Assemble a portfolio whose artifacts, statement, revision evidence, publication design, and presentation form one coherent argument.
  • Audit alignment across every portfolio component.
  • Resolve contradictions, gaps, and accessibility risks before submission.
  • Defend final readiness with evidence rather than confidence alone.

Why This Matters

Creative writing helps you communicate ideas, experiences, and perspectives with purpose. Each lesson strengthens your ability to read like a writer, make deliberate craft choices, revise thoughtfully, and explain how those choices affect a reader. These skills build creative confidence, clear communication, and responsible participation in a writing community.

What You Will Do

  • Learn and apply the lesson vocabulary.
  • Follow step-by-step instruction and study worked examples.
  • Practice through interactive checks and guided application.
  • Complete Independent Work to apply the lesson skills.
  • Complete a separate Checkpoint to demonstrate your understanding.

Lesson Workflow

  1. Complete Pages 1–4 in order.
  2. Complete Page 5 and submit it with your Page 2 vocabulary in Notebook Evidence Submission.
  3. Complete Page 6 and submit it separately in Checkpoint Submission.
  4. Review TOR feedback, correct errors, and resubmit any work scoring below 80%.
  5. Complete the assessment listed after the lesson. A score of at least 80% is required.

page.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 7 | Page 2 of 6

Vocabulary and Definitions

Notebook Task: Record every core term and its complete meaning in your notebook. Submit these vocabulary notes with your Independent Work as Notebook Evidence. Use the examples to see how each term works in context. Reference glossary terms do not need to be copied.
TermMeaningExample
coherenceThe quality of all parts connecting logically and purposefully.The artifact order and notes create one clear portfolio argument.
alignmentA clear match among goals, evidence, explanations, design, and criteria.The stated goal is supported by the selected drafts and reflection.
cross-referenceA direction connecting one component to related evidence elsewhere.The note directs readers to the marked revision on page six.
artifact mapA visual record showing what each portfolio item demonstrates and where evidence appears.The map links every criterion to a named artifact.
gap analysisA systematic search for missing evidence, skills, or requirements.The review reveals no artifact demonstrates collaboration.
quality assurancePlanned checking that confirms a product meets standards and functions as intended.The writer tests links and verifies labels before release.
provenanceDocumented information about the origin, ownership, and history of a work or media element.The image record names its creator, source, and license.
release candidateA near-final version considered ready pending a last verification pass.Version 8 becomes the release candidate after revisions.
readiness defenseAn evidence-based argument that a portfolio satisfies required criteria.The defense cites the map, revision trail, and accessibility check.

Vocabulary in Action

Match each clue to the precise term. Choose Check, study any mismatch, and retry. This practice is ungraded.

Make the Vocabulary Work

Which finding belongs in a gap analysis?

A. “The title page uses the correct font.”

This is a quality-assurance check, but it does not identify missing evidence.

B. “The portfolio claims growth in dialogue, but no paired drafts show a dialogue revision.”

Correct. It identifies a specific mismatch between a claim and the evidence needed to support it.

page.title: Lesson
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 7 | Page 3 of 6

Lesson: Integrate, Audit, and Defend the Portfolio

Step 1 — Freeze the Inventory

List every required component, its final file name, version date, standard demonstrated, and current status. Work only from this inventory so an outdated draft cannot replace an approved artifact.

Step 2 — Build the Alignment Matrix

ComponentMust align withFailure signal
ArtifactSelection rationale and standardsClaim names a skill not visible in work
Revision trailFinal version and feedbackBefore/after samples are unrelated
Author statementExact craft evidenceVague growth claim
PresentationRepresentative excerptSummary replaces analysis

Pause and Choose: Detect an Alignment Gap

The selection rationale claims a story demonstrates controlled point of view, but its evidence discusses only punctuation corrections. What should the writer do?

A. Replace the evidence with a specific point-of-view choice or revise the claim so it accurately matches what the artifact demonstrates.
Stronger choice. Portfolio coherence requires a traceable relationship between criterion, claim, and evidence. Either side may change, but they must align.
B. Keep both because any revision evidence supports any craft claim.
Weaker choice. Unrelated evidence does not verify the claim. It creates the appearance of support without demonstrating the named skill.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Step 3 — Run Gap Analysis

  1. Highlight every rubric criterion.
  2. Point to exact evidence satisfying it.
  3. Mark unsupported claims and duplicated evidence.
  4. Find missing range, growth, access, rights, or presentation evidence.
  5. Assign a corrective action, owner, and deadline—even if you are all three.

Step 4 — Audit in Independent Passes

  • Craft: quality, purpose, and range.
  • Revision: before/after accuracy and reasoning.
  • Coherence: titles, claims, cross-references, and order.
  • Publication: metadata, files, links, rights, and privacy.
  • Accessibility: contrast, headings, descriptions, captions, transcripts.
  • Presentation: excerpt, timing, visuals, and rehearsal.

Step 5 — Create the Release Candidate

Export the exact files a reader will receive. Open them outside the editing environment, follow every navigation path, and compare displayed content to the inventory.

Pause and Choose: Defend Readiness

Which final judgment is supported by a genuine quality-assurance argument?

A. “The portfolio is ready because everything looks good to me.”
Weaker choice. The statement gives no criterion, evidence, verification method, or acknowledged limitation.
B. “The portfolio meets the growth criterion through two verified before-and-after pairs; all release files passed link and display tests, though the poetry sample still shows a deliberate narrow range of forms.”
Stronger choice. It names criteria, points to evidence, reports verification, acknowledges a limitation, and reaches a proportionate judgment.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Step 6 — Defend Readiness

Use Criterion → Evidence → Verification → Limitation → Final judgment. “Everything looks good” is not a quality-assurance argument.

page.title: Worked Example
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 7 | Page 4 of 6

Worked Example: Three Integration Failures

Example 1 — Statement/Artifact Mismatch

Claim: The author statement praises controlled second-person narration. Artifact: The final story is entirely first person because the writer changed viewpoint after feedback.

  1. Diagnosis: the statement describes an obsolete version.
  2. Verify the revision trail and final file.
  3. Update the statement to analyze first-person distance and explain the viewpoint change.
  4. Cross-reference the exact before/after passage.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which repair best resolves the mismatch between the author statement and final story?

A. Keep the statement because it explains the writer’s original intention, even though the final story is first person.
Weaker response. An author statement must represent the submitted artifact; describing an obsolete version makes the portfolio internally inconsistent.
B. Update the statement to analyze first-person distance, explain why feedback prompted the viewpoint change, and cross-reference the exact before-and-after passage.
Stronger response. This repair verifies the revision trail, aligns the claim with the final artifact, and preserves evidence of the writer’s decision-making.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Example 2 — Revision Evidence Mismatch

Problem: The portfolio says pacing improved, but the before/after evidence shows only corrected punctuation.

  1. Return to revision history.
  2. Select a passage showing scene expansion, compression, or reordering.
  3. Explain how the change alters reader time and attention.
  4. If no evidence exists, qualify the growth claim rather than manufacturing proof.

Example 3 — Release-Candidate Failure

Problem: The web portfolio works in the editor, but the exported folder contains a broken audio link, an unlabeled image, and “Final3” rather than the approved final poem.

  1. Compare every file to the frozen inventory.
  2. Replace the obsolete poem and update metadata.
  3. Embed or relink the audio using a stable path and provide a transcript.
  4. Add meaningful alternative text.
  5. Re-export and test from a clean browser.

Transfer Principle

A portfolio is a system: a failure of alignment, version, access, or navigation can weaken otherwise excellent writing.

Your Turn Before Independent Work

Pause and try: A portfolio note describes a deleted ending. Write a two-step repair plan.

Check your thinking — open after you try
Teacher model: First verify the final file and revision history. Then replace the obsolete claim with an explanation of the current ending and cite the revision that produced it.

page.title: Independent Work
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 7 | Page 5 of 6

Independent Work: Integrated Author Portfolio Preparation

Purpose

Integrate selection, revision, author reflection, publication design, and presentation into a unified author portfolio.

Complete each numbered part in your notebook. Support decisions with precise evidence from your portfolio work.

Source for Your Work

Portfolio audit: Strong pieces alone do not guarantee a strong portfolio. Selection, sequence, framing, consistency, accessibility, and reflection must create a coherent experience for the reader.

1. Plan Before You Work

Portfolio DecisionEvidence and Plan
Purpose and intended audienceState each precisely.
Strongest current evidenceName the piece, passage, or feature.
Most important improvementDescribe the needed change and intended effect.

2. Choose and Explain

Which approach demonstrates stronger author decision-making? Record A or B, then explain your choice in 2–3 sentences using a lesson concept.

A. Finish each component separately and place everything together at the end without reconsidering the reader’s path.
B. Develop a controlling portfolio purpose, test how every component supports it, and revise transitions and framing so the collection functions as a whole.

3. Apply the Lesson

Assemble a complete portfolio prototype containing three polished works, an author statement, craft rationales, contents/navigation, publication formatting, and a presentation plan. Include an evidence-based readiness audit for each component.

4. Revise with Purpose

Ask what a first-time reader would understand about you as an author. Revise one sequencing choice and one framing element to make that answer clearer.

Before You Submit

  • All four numbered parts are complete.
  • Your work applies the lesson skill to specific portfolio evidence.
  • Your explanation identifies a decision and its effect on the audience.
  • Your revision meaningfully improves quality, coherence, or readiness.

page.title: Checkpoint
page.contents:
Checkpoint: Integrated Author Portfolio Preparation

Put the lesson together through analysis, decision-making, writing, and purposeful revision.

Purpose

Show that you can understand the lesson concept, apply it in original work, and explain your decisions. Complete every numbered item and submit your responses with your Checkpoint work.

New Source: The Coherent Author

A portfolio moves from a restrained poem about departure to a tense short story about returning, then to a monologue spoken by someone who refuses to leave. The forms differ, yet repeated doorway images and increasingly complex choices create a coherent conversation across the works.

An integrated portfolio creates intentional relationships among selection, sequence, revision, design, author statement, and presentation. Coherence does not require sameness; it requires meaningful connection.

Part 1: Analyze the Source

  1. How do form, sequence, repeated imagery, and character choices create coherence without making the pieces repetitive?
  2. What evidence should the author statement and presentation highlight to help readers recognize the portfolio’s design?

Use this response pattern: Make a precise claim, cite the relevant detail, and explain how the detail proves the claim.

Part 2: Choose A or B

3. Which approach produces mature portfolio coherence?

A. Make every piece use the same narrator, setting, and ending so the collection cannot feel inconsistent.
B. Preserve meaningful range while using sequence, recurring concerns, craft development, and contextual notes to create connection.

Record A or B in your submission and explain your choice in 2–3 sentences. The answer is not revealed here because this item is part of your graded written work.

Part 3: Create and Apply

4. Assemble an integrated author portfolio draft with at least four polished works in two or more forms.

  1. Curate: Select for quality, range, growth, and an identifiable throughline.
  2. Revise: Complete and document one major revision for every piece.
  3. Sequence: Arrange the collection to create an intentional reader journey.
  4. Frame: Add a polished author statement and 100–150 word context note for each work.
  5. Prepare: Apply the publication system and draft the author presentation.

Write a 250–300 word integration rationale explaining how selection, sequence, revision, design, and presentation operate as one project.

Plan before drafting: Decide what the audience should understand, how each section will build that understanding, and which details will do the most work.

Part 4: Revise With Purpose

5. Audit the portfolio as a whole. Make one revision to sequence, one to framing, and one to visual consistency; explain the effect of each.

Do more than correct spelling. Revise organization, meaning, evidence, or craft so the work becomes clearer and more effective.

Before You Submit

  • Every numbered item is complete.
  • Analysis includes specific evidence and reasoning.
  • The creative work follows the required organization and length.
  • The A/B response is recorded and explained.
  • The revision is visible and its purpose is clear.

Mastery Target

A score of 80% or higher demonstrates mastery. Depth, control, and application matter more than unnecessary length.

TOR Help

If you are unsure how to organize your response, choose evidence, or revise meaningfully, contact your Teacher of Record before submitting.
